opening_message:
Ticket 1: Christopher Myers (employee ID E012) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E012.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Christopher Myers (E012) is a full-time Analyst requesting write access to Source Code. As a full-time employee, write is permitted (admin is only for the owning Engineer role). Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E012 (Christopher Myers) is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time as previously noted. Contractors with basic training max out at read. Requested write to Source Code exceeds max, so recommend granting read.
reason: Requested write access to Source Code. The Security note indicates E012 (Christopher Myers) is a contractor with basic security training (per Security DB lookup), which limits contractors to read unless they have advanced security training. Write is above the maximum for this contractor, so the maximum (read) is granted.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: Christopher Myers (E012)
Requested: write access to Source Code

Two notes:
- Note 1 (HR-ish): role Analyst, employment type full_time, recommends write for Source Code.
- Note 2 (Security): role Analyst, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommends read. Comment says Security DB shows contractor with basic training, max read.

Conflict: employment type full_time vs contractor.

Access policy:
1. full_time: up to write; admin only if role owns the system. Source Code is owned by Engineer role. Analyst is not Engineer, so max write for full-time.
2. contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If full-time: requested write is allowed → grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max read → grant read.

The Security agent says they looked up in own database employment type contractor and security training basic. Note 2 says employment type not looked up... wait, note 2 says "role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)" but "employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)" and "security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)".

So the Security agent looked up the employment type in their own database and found contractor. Note 1 (from HR?) says full_time but note 2 corrects that based on their database lookup.

The security agent's note is more specifically about employment type and training, having looked it up. The first note's employment type may not have been verified? Actually note 1 says "employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)" - but whose database? Hmm. Both notes claim lookups.

The discrepancy is which database is authoritative. The Security agent explicitly says "Security DB shows E012 is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time as previously noted." This suggests the Security DB is the authoritative source for employment type, and it contradicts the earlier claim.

The team memory has both notes. As Approver, I need to decide. Given the conflict, the more reliable/updated info seems to be the Security database: contractor with basic training. That means max is read (contractors without advanced training max read).

Requested write > max read → grant read.

Let me submit decision: read.
